label: Sheet resistance and counting squares
lesson:
# Sheet resistance and counting squares

Every resistance an extractor reports starts from the same idea: a metal layer of fixed thickness has a sheet resistance, and a wire's resistance is that number times how many squares of its own width fit along it. The extractor never needs absolute dimensions for this, only ratios, which is why process kits publish sheet resistance per layer. Getting the square count right on straight runs, width changes and corners is the first thing a resistance extractor does after it has fractured a net into rectangles.

## Resistance per square

A wire of resistivity $\rho$, thickness $T$, width $W$ and length $L$ has $R = \rho L / (W T)$. Group the terms as $R = (\rho / T)(L / W)$. The first factor, $R_s = \rho/T$, depends only on the layer and is called the sheet resistance, in ohms per square. The second, $L/W$, is the number of squares: how many $W \times W$ tiles fit along the wire. A square of any size has the same resistance, because doubling its side doubles the path length and the cross-section together. A wire 2.4 um long and 0.02 um wide holds $2.4/0.02 = 120$ squares. Counting squares is pure geometry, so an extractor can do it on the fractured rectangles before it knows anything about temperature or corner.

## From resistivity to ohms

When a process gives resistivity and thickness instead of sheet resistance, form $R_s = \rho/T$ first. With an effective resistivity of 0.04 ohm-um and a thickness of 0.08 um, $R_s = 0.5$ ohm/sq. A wire 32 um long and 0.2 um wide has 160 squares, so $R = 0.5 \times 160 = 80$ ohm. Series segments add: a net that runs 100 squares on one layer and 40 on another of different sheet resistance sums the two products. A width change along the wire simply splits it into two rectangles with their own square counts. The word effective matters: at advanced nodes the resistivity a kit quotes already includes the size effects that raise copper resistivity above its bulk value, so it is a per-layer, sometimes per-width, number rather than a constant of nature.

## Corners and current crowding

At a right-angle bend the current does not use the corner square uniformly. It crowds around the inner corner and leaves the outer corner nearly idle, so the corner square conducts better than one full square. The standard approximation counts a corner square of an L-shaped wire as about 0.56 squares. For an L of width 0.02 um whose arms hold 190 and 20 squares outside the corner, with $R_s = 0.5$ ohm/sq, the resistance is $0.5 \times (190 + 20 + 0.56) = 105.28$ ohm. Treating the corner as a full square, or as zero, misses by a few tenths of a square per bend, which is small on long wires but noticeable on short, jogged local nets with many bends. Extractors handle bends, T-junctions and contacts with precomputed correction tables for exactly this reason.

## Going deeper

Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed., 2011), the chapter on interconnect; Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed., 2003), chapter 4.

label: Wire and via resistance
lesson:
# Wire and via resistance

A routed net is a chain of wire segments on several layers joined by vias. Its resistance is the series sum of every segment and every via level, with parallel via cuts dividing a via level's resistance. At advanced nodes the vias, not the wires, often dominate short nets. The extractor computes this sum from fractured geometry and the layer stack, and the result feeds every delay and IR-drop calculation downstream, so a misplaced via array or a wrong per-cut value propagates straight into timing.

## Resistance from dimensions

The resistance of one wire segment is $R = \rho L/(W T)$, with the effective resistivity $\rho$ of its layer. Keep all lengths in micrometres and $\rho$ in ohm-um, and the units cancel to ohms. A copper segment with $\rho = 0.025$ ohm-um, $W = 0.04$ um, $T = 0.05$ um and $L = 120$ um has $R = 0.025 \times 120 / (0.04 \times 0.05) = 1500$ ohm. That is large: minimum-width lower metal at advanced nodes reaches tens of ohms per micrometre, which is why long nets are promoted to thicker upper layers. The extractor reads $W$ from the drawn geometry, corrected for the process bias, and $T$ from the layer stack in the technology file; both shift with the extraction corner.

## Vias in series and in parallel

Each via level a net crosses adds the resistance of its cut, or of its cut array. Identical cuts in parallel divide: four cuts of 50 ohm give 12.5 ohm. A route that runs 190 squares on M2 at 1.5 ohm/sq (285 ohm), crosses one via level through four 50 ohm cuts (12.5 ohm), and runs 60 squares on M3 at 0.5 ohm/sq (30 ohm) totals $285 + 12.5 + 30 = 327.5$ ohm. A net that climbs from M1 to M5 crosses four via levels on the way up and four on the way down, so its via resistance is eight per-level values. Redundant vias, inserted by the router or a post-route step, both lower resistance and protect against a single failed cut, which is why via doubling is a yield and reliability step as much as a timing one.

## When vias dominate

On a short connection the vias can outweigh the wire. A net that climbs two single-cut via levels of 55 ohm each, runs 170 squares at 1 ohm/sq, and descends two levels has 170 ohm of wire and 220 ohm of vias: 56% of its resistance is in the vias. Two consequences follow for tool design. First, a router that minimizes wirelength alone can make a net slower by adding layer changes, so via count must be in the cost function. Second, the extractor must model each via level separately, with the cut count and the landing geometry, rather than lumping vias into a per-net constant. Via resistance also has its own corner variation, independent of metal width, which signoff corners must cover.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design: From Graph Partitioning to Timing Closure" (2nd ed., 2022), the chapters on routing and timing; the IRDS interconnect roadmap tables for resistance trends.

label: Temperature dependence of wire resistance
prereqs: Elmore delay of an RC tree
lesson:
# Temperature dependence of wire resistance

Metal resistance rises with temperature, roughly linearly over the operating range. An extractor reports resistance at a stated temperature, and signoff corners run from cold to hot, so the same geometry yields different resistances per corner. The temperature coefficient is the knob, and a tool designer has to know which numbers scale with it and which, like the driver resistance characterized in a cell library, are handled elsewhere.

## The linear temperature coefficient

Over the range chips operate in, metal resistance follows $R(T) = R_0[1 + \alpha (T - T_0)]$, where $R_0$ is the value at a reference temperature $T_0$ (often 25 C) and $\alpha$ is the temperature coefficient of resistance, on the order of 3 to $4 \times 10^{-3}$ per C for copper interconnect. A wire of 160 ohm at 25 C with $\alpha = 0.003$ per C measures $160 \times (1 + 0.003 \times 85) = 200.8$ ohm at 110 C, a 25% increase. Some technology files also carry a quadratic term; the linear form is the one most often used. Vias and barrier materials have their own coefficients, so an extractor applies them per layer and per via type.

## Moving between corners

Extraction results are often stored at one temperature and rescaled for another. To move from a hot value to a cold one, first recover the reference value, then scale again. A net reported at 620.4 ohm at 125 C with $\alpha = 0.0032$ per C has $R_{25} = 620.4/(1 + 0.0032 \times 100) = 470$ ohm, and at -40 C it becomes $470 \times (1 - 0.0032 \times 65) = 372.24$ ohm. The two-step route matters: scaling directly by the ratio of the two bracketed factors gives the same answer, but scaling by $\alpha \Delta T$ relative to the hot value does not, because the coefficient is defined against $R_0$. A tool that writes SPEF per corner bakes this in; a tool that rescales on the fly must carry the reference temperature with every value.

## What scales and what does not

Only the interconnect resistance in the parasitic netlist follows the wire coefficient. A cell's drive strength is characterized in the library at each corner, and the timer picks the library that matches the corner, so the extractor does not scale it. Consider a net whose Elmore delay at 25 C splits into a 26 ps driver term and a 27 ps wire term. With $\alpha = 0.0032$ per C at 125 C, only the wire term grows, to 35.64 ps, giving 61.64 ps. Wire-dominated nets, the long ones, are the most temperature sensitive. Because transistors may get faster or slower with temperature depending on supply voltage, the hot corner is not automatically the slowest for every path, and signoff runs both ends of the range.

## Going deeper

The temperature sections of an Interconnect Technology Format description in a process design kit; Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed., 2003), chapter 4.

label: Barrier layers and size effects in copper
lesson:
# Barrier layers and size effects in copper

A modern copper wire is not all copper. A thin barrier liner, needed to stop copper diffusing into the dielectric, coats its sides and bottom and conducts poorly. And as wires shrink toward the electron mean free path, surface and grain-boundary scattering raise copper's resistivity. Both effects grow as wires narrow, so an extractor's resistance model at advanced nodes must use the conducting cross-section and a width-dependent resistivity rather than the drawn rectangle and a constant.

## The conducting cross-section

In a damascene copper process the barrier, often tantalum-based, lines both sidewalls and the bottom of the trench. If the barrier is $b$ thick and conducts negligibly, the copper occupies $(W - 2b)(T - b)$ of the drawn $W \times T$. A wire 0.05 um wide and 0.04 um thick with a 0.004 um barrier keeps $0.042 \times 0.036 = 0.001512$ um$^2$ of copper out of 0.002 um$^2$: only 75.6%. The barrier does not shrink at the same rate as the wire, because it must stay thick enough to block diffusion, so its share of the cross-section grows at each node. This is one of the main reasons resistance per unit length has risen much faster than simple scaling predicts.

## Resistance penalty of the liner

Resistance goes as one over the conducting area, so the liner raises it by the ratio of drawn to copper area. For a wire 0.03 um wide and 0.08 um thick with a 0.003 um barrier, the copper area is $0.024 \times 0.077 = 0.001848$ um$^2$ against 0.0024 drawn, a ratio of 1.2987: the barrier alone adds 29.9% to the resistance. Narrow wires suffer most, because the sidewall term $2b$ is a larger fraction of a small width. An extractor that uses drawn dimensions with bulk resistivity would under-report resistance by this factor. In practice the technology file either describes the barrier explicitly or folds it into an effective resistivity per width, and the extractor must apply whichever convention the file uses, never both.

## Width-dependent resistivity

When the copper width approaches the electron mean free path (about 40 nm in bulk copper at room temperature), electrons scatter off surfaces and grain boundaries more often, and resistivity rises. A simple model writes $\rho = \rho_0 (1 + K/W_c)$ with $W_c$ the copper width. With $\rho_0 = 0.018$ ohm-um and $K = 0.02$ um, a wire drawn 0.04 um wide with a 0.003 um barrier has $W_c = 0.034$ um and $\rho = 0.0286$ ohm-um. For 40 um of length and 0.057 um of copper height, $R = 0.0286 \times 40 / 0.001938 = 590$ ohm. Real models (Fuchs-Sondheimer for surfaces, Mayadas-Shatzkes for grains) are more detailed, and foundries tabulate the result per layer and width. The point for tool design is that resistivity is a function of geometry the extractor must look up, not a constant.

## Going deeper

Gall, "Electron mean free path in elemental metals", Journal of Applied Physics (2016); the IRDS interconnect chapter on resistivity scaling and alternative metals.

label: Area capacitance to the layer below
lesson:
# Area capacitance to the layer below

The simplest capacitance a wire has is the parallel-plate part: the field running straight down from its bottom face to a wide conductor below, such as the substrate or a dense layer of crossing wires. It is the first term in every extraction model and the one a back-of-envelope estimate uses. Understanding how it scales with width, dielectric thickness and permittivity tells a tool designer why area capacitance alone has become a poor estimate at advanced nodes.

## The parallel-plate formula

Two parallel conducting plates of area $A$, separated by $h$ of a dielectric with relative permittivity $\varepsilon_r$, have $C = \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r A / h$, ignoring the field that bulges out at the edges. For a wire, $A = W L$. In micrometre units, $\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-3}$ fF/um. A wire 1 um wide and 180 um long, 0.1 um above a ground plane in a dielectric with $\varepsilon_r = 2.5$, has $C = 0.008854 \times 2.5 \times 1 \times 180 / 0.1 = 39.84$ fF. Silicon dioxide has $\varepsilon_r \approx 3.9$; low-k interlayer dielectrics are lower, which is why they were introduced: capacitance falls in proportion.

## Capacitance per unit length

Extraction tables and wire-load estimates work per unit length, because a wire's cross-section repeats along it. Per micron, $C/L = \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r W / h$. A 1 um wire 0.05 um above its plane in $\varepsilon_r = 3$ gives $0.008854 \times 3 / 0.05 = 0.531$ fF/um, or 531 aF/um. Attofarads per micron (1 aF = $10^{-3}$ fF) are the natural unit for minimum-width wires, whose total capacitance per micron is typically of order 0.1 to 0.2 fF, that is 100 to 200 aF. Per-length values let an extractor multiply by the parallel run length of each fractured segment instead of solving the field again.

## Scaling and its limits

Area capacitance goes as $\varepsilon_r W / h$. If a shrink scales width by 0.5 and dielectric height by 0.8 with the same material, area capacitance per length falls to $0.5/0.8 = 0.625$ of its old value. That looks like progress, but the wire's sides have not shrunk as much as its width: thickness is kept up to control resistance, so the sidewalls become a larger share of the wire's surface. The parallel-plate term then underestimates the true capacitance badly, because fringe fields from the sidewalls and coupling to neighbours dominate. This is why total capacitance per unit length has stayed roughly constant across many nodes, and why extractors must model fringe and coupling explicitly.

label: Fringe capacitance
prereqs: Area capacitance to the layer below
lesson:
# Fringe capacitance

The field from a wire does not stop at its bottom face. Field lines leave its sidewalls and top and curve down to the conductor below, adding fringe capacitance along each edge. For narrow wires this fringe term is larger than the area term, so any extraction model that is accurate at advanced nodes is mainly a model of fringing. Extractors separate the two because they scale differently: area capacitance with width, fringe with length alone.

## Area plus edges

A practical model writes a wire's capacitance to ground as an area term plus a fringe term per edge: $C = c_a W L + 2 c_f L$, where $c_a$ is in aF/um$^2$ and $c_f$ in aF/um per edge. The fringe term does not depend on width, because the fringing field near an edge looks the same whether the wire is wide or narrow, once it is wider than a few dielectric thicknesses. A wire 0.05 um wide and 180 um long with $c_a = 80$ aF/um$^2$ and $c_f = 75$ aF/um has area capacitance $80 \times 0.05 \times 180 = 720$ aF and fringe $2 \times 75 \times 180 = 27000$ aF: 27.72 fF in total, almost all of it fringe. Such coefficients come from field-solver runs, fitted per layer.

## The fringe share

The fraction of ground capacitance that is fringe is $2c_f/(c_a W + 2c_f)$, independent of length. For $W = 0.05$ um, $c_a = 80$ aF/um$^2$ and $c_f = 30$ aF/um, the area term is 4 aF/um and the fringe 60 aF/um: 93.8% fringe. Width sizing therefore changes capacitance much less than the parallel-plate formula suggests: doubling the width of this wire adds only 4 aF/um, under 7%, while halving its resistance. This asymmetry is why wide wires are effective for long nets and why sizing a wire to cut delay does not cost proportionally more capacitance. It also explains why extraction errors in fringe models matter more than errors in area models.

## The crossover width

Fringe exceeds area capacitance when $c_a W < 2 c_f$, that is below the width $W^* = 2c_f/c_a$. With $c_a = 20$ aF/um$^2$ and $c_f = 80$ aF/um per edge, $W^* = 8$ um. Every signal wire at an advanced node is far below such a crossover, so its ground capacitance is dominated by edges. The model's assumption that $c_f$ is width-independent fails for very narrow wires, where the two edges' fringe fields interact, and in dense wiring, where neighbours intercept fringe lines and turn them into coupling. Production extractors therefore tabulate fringe against neighbour spacing too, rather than using one constant per layer.

## Going deeper

Sakurai and Tamaru, "Simple formulas for two- and three-dimensional capacitances", IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices (1983); Cheng, Lillis, Lin and Chang, "Interconnect Analysis and Synthesis" (2000).

label: Coupling capacitance
prereqs: Area capacitance to the layer below
lesson:
# Coupling capacitance

Two wires side by side form a capacitor through the dielectric between their facing sidewalls. This coupling capacitance does not go to ground: its other terminal is another signal, so its effect on delay and noise depends on what that neighbour is doing. As wires got taller and closer, coupling became the largest component of many nets' capacitance, and extracting it per neighbour, rather than lumping it into ground, is what makes signal-integrity analysis possible.

## Facing sidewalls

The facing sidewalls of two parallel wires of thickness $T$, spaced $s$ apart along a run of length $L$, behave roughly like parallel plates: $C_c \approx \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r T L / s$. Two wires 0.05 um thick at 0.05 um spacing for 30 um in $\varepsilon_r = 2.5$ give $0.008854 \times 2.5 \times 0.05 \times 30 / 0.05 = 0.66$ fF. Fringing between top corners adds to this, so field solvers report more. The formula shows why coupling grew with scaling: wires are kept tall to limit resistance (aspect ratios of 2 or more), so $T/s$ rises as pitch shrinks. Coupling is then often more than half of a minimum-pitch wire's total capacitance.

## Spacing dependence

Coupling per length falls as spacing grows, roughly as $1/s$ in the plate model, faster when the extra space lets field lines escape to ground instead. Characterization tables give coupling at several spacings, and the extractor interpolates. If a table gives 95 aF/um at 0.04 um and the model is $1/s$, two wires at 0.08 um couple 47.5 aF/um; over 250 um that is 11.875 fF. Doubling the spacing halves coupling but does not shrink total capacitance by as much, because some of the field lines that ended on the neighbour now end on the ground below as fringe. This is the physical basis of the spacing-based crosstalk fix that routers apply to critical nets.

## Parallel run length

Two wires couple only where they run side by side. The extractor finds, for each pair of neighbouring segments, the interval along the track direction where both exist: the overlap of their extents. A victim from $x = 0$ to 90 um and an aggressor from $x = 10$ to 150 um on the adjacent track overlap from 10 to 90, 80 um. At 150 aF/um this gives 12 fF. Computing overlaps for every pair is a geometric sweep: sort segments by position along each track and scan neighbouring tracks together, which is $O(n \log n)$ rather than all pairs. End effects, where the field wraps around a line end, add a small correction that pattern libraries handle separately.

label: The Maxwell capacitance matrix
lesson:
# The Maxwell capacitance matrix

A set of conductors over ground is described exactly, in electrostatics, by its capacitance matrix: the linear map from conductor voltages to conductor charges. Field solvers output it, extractors read ground and coupling capacitances out of it, and confusing its sign conventions is a classic integration bug. A tool designer needs to read the matrix fluently in both directions: from matrix to circuit elements, and from elements back to the matrix.

## Couplings off the diagonal

For $N$ conductors with voltages $V$ relative to ground, the charges are $Q = C V$, where $C$ is the Maxwell capacitance matrix. Entry $C_{ij}$ for $i \ne j$ is the charge induced on conductor $i$ when conductor $j$ is at 1 V and all others at 0 V. That charge is negative: raising one conductor pulls opposite charge onto its grounded neighbours. The circuit coupling capacitance between $i$ and $j$ is therefore $-C_{ij}$, a positive number. If row 2 of a three-conductor matrix is $[-8, 17, -2]$ fF, conductor 2 couples 8 fF to conductor 1 and 2 fF to conductor 3. The matrix is symmetric by reciprocity, so $C_{23} = C_{32}$ is a free sanity check on a solver run.

## Ground capacitance as a row sum

Put every conductor at 1 V. Nothing then differs in voltage between conductors, so the couplings carry no charge, and conductor $i$ holds only the charge on its capacitance to ground, $C_{gi}$. But by the matrix, its charge is $\sum_j C_{ij}$, the row sum. So the ground capacitance is the row sum. For row 3, $[-4, -2, 10]$ fF, ground capacitance is $-4 - 2 + 10 = 4$ fF. If a design has no explicit ground conductor, rows sum to zero, which signals that the reference was chosen as one of the conductors. Extraction tools convert the matrix into a netlist of grounded and coupling capacitors by exactly these two rules.

## Building the diagonal

Going the other way, the diagonal entry is the total capacitance of the conductor: its ground capacitance plus all its couplings, $C_{ii} = C_{gi} + \sum_{j \ne i} C_{c,ij}$. With ground capacitances of 2, 8 and 2 fF and couplings of 5 (1 to 2), 6 (1 to 3) and 8 fF (2 to 3), $C_{33} = 2 + 6 + 8 = 16$ fF. This is the load a driver of conductor 3 sees when every neighbour is held still. The matrix is diagonally dominant and positive definite, properties that solvers and reducers rely on. A common bug is mixing this Maxwell form with the mutual form that some tools report, where off-diagonals are positive coupling values and diagonals are ground capacitances only.

## Going deeper

Jackson, "Classical Electrodynamics" (3rd ed., 1999), the section on capacitance coefficients; Nabors and White, "FastCap: a multipole accelerated 3-D capacitance extraction program", IEEE Transactions on CAD (1991).

label: Total capacitance of a net
lesson:
# Total capacitance of a net

A driver's load is the sum of everything it must charge: wire capacitance to ground, coupling to every neighbour, and the input capacitance of every sink pin. Extractors report these components separately so that downstream tools can treat them differently. A timer without signal-integrity analysis grounds the couplings; a crosstalk analyser keeps them as couplings; nothing should drop them. Assembling the total, and knowing what share of it is coupling, is the first step of any delay or noise reasoning about a net.

## Summing the components

A net's capacitance is wire ground capacitance (area plus fringe) plus coupling to each neighbour plus pin capacitance: $C_{tot} = L(c_g + c_{c,1} + c_{c,2}) + \sum C_{pin}$, using per-length values for a uniform wire. A 40 um net with 112 aF/um to ground, 22 and 61 aF/um of coupling to its two neighbours, and two pins of 0.5 and 1.1 fF has $40 \times 195 = 7800$ aF of wire, 7.8 fF, plus 1.6 fF of pins: 9.4 fF. Counting coupling at face value, as if the neighbours were grounded, is the quiet-neighbour assumption, Miller factor 1. Pin capacitance comes from the Liberty library, not from extraction, and the timer adds it when it combines the two.

## The coupling share

The fraction of a net's capacitance that is coupling tells how sensitive it is to its neighbours. A 200 um net with 79 aF/um to ground, 64 and 48 aF/um of coupling, and 4.6 fF of pins has 22.4 fF of coupling out of 42.8 fF: 52%. At that share, an aggressor switching against the victim can almost double the effective coupling load, which moves delay by tens of percent. Extractors and routers track this ratio: a high coupling share flags a net for spacing, shielding or a crosstalk-aware timing check. Long parallel runs at minimum spacing on the same layer, typical of buses, push the share highest.

## Grounded versus dropped coupling

Without SI analysis, a timer grounds each coupling capacitor: it keeps the capacitance but forgets which net is on the other side. That preserves the total load. A flow that instead drops coupling, keeping only ground and pin capacitance, under-reports load by the full coupling: for a 260 um net with 96 aF/um of coupling, that is 24.96 fF out of 40.82 fF, a huge optimistic error. Real flows lose coupling by accident through format conversions, filtering thresholds that discard small couplings without regrounding them, or incomplete SPEF reads. A robust extractor offers decoupling with regrounding as an explicit mode, and a robust timer checks that each net's total matches its header.

## Going deeper

label: Field-solver capacitance extraction
prereqs: The method of moments field solver
lesson:
# Field-solver capacitance extraction

A field solver computes capacitance from first principles: it solves the electrostatic potential around a set of conductors and integrates the resulting surface charges. It is the golden reference against which every fast extractor is calibrated, and the engine used directly on the few nets where accuracy matters most. Knowing what it computes, how its output is read, and what makes its results trustworthy is the foundation for every other extraction method.

## What the solver computes

Between conductors there is no free charge, so the potential $\phi$ satisfies Laplace's equation, $\nabla \cdot (\varepsilon \nabla \phi) = 0$, with $\phi$ fixed on each conductor's surface. Once $\phi$ is known, the surface charge density is $\sigma = -\varepsilon\, \partial \phi / \partial n$ on each conductor, and integrating it gives the conductor's charge. Because charge is linear in the boundary voltages, $Q = C V$. To get the full capacitance matrix of $N$ conductors, the solver runs $N$ solves, each with one conductor at 1 V and the rest at 0 V, and records all $N$ charges as one column. At on-chip sizes the structures are tiny compared with a wavelength, so this quasi-static electric problem is the whole capacitance story.

## Reading a solve

A solve with conductor 1 at 1 V reports charges in fC per volt, which are capacitances in fF. Suppose conductor 1 carries 8 fC and conductors 2 and 3 carry -0.75 and -2.75 fC. The driven conductor's charge is its total capacitance, $C_{11} = 8$ fF. The negative charges on the others are the negated couplings: 0.75 fF to conductor 2 and 2.75 fF to conductor 3. Charge conservation puts the remaining $8 - 0.75 - 2.75 = 4.5$ fC of negative charge on the ground plane, so the ground capacitance of conductor 1 is 4.5 fF. Field-solver post-processing does exactly this bookkeeping, and the coupling values it produces must stay attached to their aggressor nets for signal-integrity analysis.

## When the reference is golden

A solver is golden only if its inputs and discretization are. Its process description, the full dielectric stack including thin etch-stop and barrier layers, must match the foundry's, or every result errs in the same direction. Its mesh must be refined until results stop changing: a 4% shift on one refinement and 0.3% on the next means the coarse mesh was not converged. Its output must pass structural checks, such as symmetry of the matrix and non-positive off-diagonals. Because a 3D solve is costly, flows use it on critical analog or clock nets and to build and verify the tables used by fast extractors, and they approximate most of the chip by 2.5D cross-section tables where wiring is locally uniform.

label: Rule-based extraction by pattern matching
lesson:
# Rule-based extraction by pattern matching

Full-chip extraction cannot solve a field problem for billions of wire segments. Production extractors instead fracture the layout into pieces, classify each piece's local cross-section as a known pattern (a wire with a neighbour at some spacing, over some layer, under another), and look up its capacitance per length in tables precomputed by a field solver. This rule-based, or pattern-matching, approach is what makes signoff extraction feasible, and its accuracy is exactly the accuracy of its tables and its interpolation.

## Table lookup along one index

A pattern table stores capacitance per length for a pattern class, indexed by geometric parameters such as wire width and spacing to the neighbour. When the query lies between table points, the extractor interpolates. Along a single index this is linear: at width 0.02 um, if coupling is 75 aF/um at spacing 0.03 um and 55 aF/um at 0.04 um, then at 0.0325 um the fraction is $t = 0.25$ and the value is $75 + 0.25 \times (55 - 75) = 70$ aF/um. The lookup is the same operation a timer performs on an NLDM table, and it carries the same caveat: linear interpolation is only as good as the table's spacing relative to the curvature of the real function, which for coupling versus spacing is strongly convex.

## Two indices and a run length

With two indices, width and spacing, the extractor interpolates bilinearly over the four surrounding table points, then multiplies by the segment's parallel run length. For a table with 97 and 82 aF/um at width 0.06 um (spacings 0.06 and 0.08 um), and 102 and 87 aF/um at width 0.08 um, the point (0.075, 0.075) has fractions 0.75 and 0.75, giving 89.5 aF/um. A 80 um run then contributes 7.16 fF of coupling. Real pattern libraries index more parameters: the layers above and below, whether they are dense or sparse, the neighbour on the other side. Each added index multiplies table size, so library design is a trade between accuracy and the cost of characterization and lookup.

## Fracturing a varying net

Real nets change environment along their length: neighbours jog away, layers above end, spacing steps. The extractor fractures a wire into segments over which the cross-section is constant, looks each up separately and sums. A 70 um segment at spacing 0.05 um (103 aF/um) followed by 130 um at 0.06 um (86 aF/um) gives $7.21 + 11.18 = 18.39$ fF of coupling. Fracturing is where 3D effects slip through: line ends, corners and vias do not match any 2D cross-section, so libraries add special 3D patterns or corrections for them. A shape that matches no pattern at all, for example a new via-rail structure, is extracted with the nearest available pattern and an unknown error, which is a strong argument for calibration checks on new layout styles.

## Going deeper

Kao, Lo, Basel and Singh, "Parasitic extraction: current state of the art and future trends", Proceedings of the IEEE (2001); the documentation of the open-source OpenRCX extractor in OpenROAD.

label: Floating random-walk capacitance solvers
lesson:
# Floating random-walk capacitance solvers

The floating random-walk method computes capacitance by Monte Carlo instead of meshing. Each walk starts near one conductor and hops through the dielectric until it lands on some conductor; averaging the walks' scores estimates a capacitance. It needs no mesh and no matrix, its memory is tiny, its accuracy is set by the number of walks, and it parallelizes almost perfectly. These properties make it a popular golden-accuracy engine in commercial extractors.

## Walks and scores

The method rests on the mean-value property of Laplace's equation: the potential at a point equals the average potential over a surrounding surface. A walk starts on a Gaussian surface around conductor $i$, jumps to a random point on the largest empty cube or sphere around its current position (sampled with the known Green's function of that shape), and repeats until it lands on a conductor. A walk ending on conductor $j$ contributes a score, a weight derived from Gauss's law at its start, to the estimate of $C_{ij}$; walks ending elsewhere contribute zero to that entry. The capacitance estimate is the sample mean. Seven walks scoring 2.2, 4, 0.9, 1.6, 3.7, 1.2 and 2.8 fF give 16.4/7 = 2.343 fF, a very rough estimate that real solvers refine with many thousands of walks.

## The standard error

Each walk is an independent sample, so the estimate's standard error is $\sigma/\sqrt{N}$, where $\sigma$ is the standard deviation of the per-walk score. With $N = 10000$ walks, mean 18 fF and $\sigma = 36$ fF, the standard error is $36/100 = 0.36$ fF, a relative error of 2%. The central limit theorem makes the estimate approximately normal, so the solver can report a confidence interval and stop when the interval is narrow enough. The per-walk standard deviation is often larger than the mean, because individual scores vary widely; it is the averaging that delivers accuracy. Variance-reduction techniques, such as better weighting or importance sampling, cut $\sigma$ and therefore the walk count for the same accuracy.

## Walks needed for a target

To reach a relative standard error $\varepsilon$, need $\sigma / \sqrt{N} \le \varepsilon \mu$, so $N \ge (\sigma / (\varepsilon \mu))^2$. With $\mu = 4.5$ fF, $\sigma = 11.25$ fF and a 2% target, $N \ge (11.25/0.09)^2 = 15625$ walks. The square is the key cost law: halving the error quadruples the work. That makes accuracy a natural tuning parameter for this engine, exactly the kind of Tier 1 setting an agent or flow can change per net class: loose for bulk signal nets, tight for clocks. Because walks are independent, the work splits across threads or machines with almost no communication, and an incremental change in geometry only requires re-running the walks for nearby conductors.

## Going deeper

Le Coz and Iverson, "A stochastic algorithm for high speed capacitance extraction in integrated circuits", Solid-State Electronics (1992); Rubinstein and Kroese, "Simulation and the Monte Carlo Method" (3rd ed., 2016), on variance reduction.

label: Boundary-element versus finite-element solvers
prereqs: The method of moments field solver
lesson:
# Boundary-element versus finite-element solvers

Deterministic field solvers come in two main families. Boundary-element methods discretize only conductor surfaces and produce small, dense systems. Finite-element and finite-difference methods mesh the whole volume and produce large, sparse systems. Each fits different structures, and an extraction engine designer must understand their unknown counts, memory and solve costs to pick and accelerate the right one.

## Surface panels

A boundary-element method (BEM), a form of the method of moments, writes the potential as an integral of unknown surface charge against the free-space Green's function. It discretizes each conductor surface into panels with a constant charge each, and enforces the known potential at each panel. The unknowns are the panel charges, so their count is the surface area divided by the panel area. A box-shaped wire 1.4 um long, 0.05 um wide and 0.15 um thick, cut into 0.05 um square panels, is $28 \times 1 \times 3$ in panel units, with $2(28 + 84 + 3) = 230$ panels. Only surfaces are meshed, so the unknown count grows with the square of feature size, not the cube.

## Dense matrices

Every panel's charge affects the potential at every other panel, so the BEM system matrix is dense: $N^2$ entries for $N$ panels. In double precision that is $8N^2$ bytes; 17000 panels need $8 \times 17000^2 = 2.3 \times 10^9$ bytes, 2312 MB. A direct LU solve costs $O(N^3)$ operations. Practical BEM extractors therefore never form the matrix: they solve iteratively with GMRES and compute matrix-vector products with acceleration such as the fast multipole method (as in FastCap) or precorrected FFT, bringing cost near $O(N)$ or $O(N \log N)$ per iteration. A preconditioner is needed to keep the iteration count low.

## Volume meshes and sparsity

A finite-element method (FEM) meshes the dielectric volume and solves for the potential at mesh nodes. Each node couples only to its neighbours, so the matrix is sparse: a tetrahedral or hexahedral mesh has on the order of 7 to 27 nonzeros per row. FEM uses many more unknowns than BEM for the same structure but far fewer per unknown. With 2000 BEM panels against 100000 FEM unknowns at 27 nonzeros each, the stored entries are $4 \times 10^6$ versus $2.7 \times 10^6$, a ratio of 1.48. FEM handles complex, layered dielectrics and nonuniform permittivity naturally, since material changes are local, whereas BEM needs a layered Green's function or extra unknowns on dielectric interfaces. Both, and random-walk methods, serve as golden references for pattern tables.

lesson:
# Calibrating extraction to a golden solver

A fast extractor is trusted only because it has been compared with a golden field solver on many structures and adjusted until the two agree within a stated tolerance. That calibration step is a small fitting problem: measure the error, fit correction coefficients, and check what error remains. It is also the step that foundries qualify, and the one that most often needs repeating when a process, a layout style or a metal stack changes.

## Measuring the error

Run the fast extractor and the golden solver on the same set of test structures or nets, and compute each relative error $|x_i - g_i| / g_i$, with $x_i$ the fast value and $g_i$ the golden one. The figures that matter are the mean error, which reveals systematic bias, and the worst-case error, which bounds what a timer can trust. For four nets with fast and golden values of 10.2 vs 9.88, 5.6 vs 5.11, 7.4 vs 6.82 and 9.9 vs 9.21 fF, the worst error is 9.59% on the second net, and every net reads high: a sign of bias, not scatter. Foundries publish accuracy targets for qualified extractors, typically a few percent on total and coupling capacitance, measured exactly this way.

## Least-squares scale factor

The simplest correction multiplies fast values by one factor $k$ per pattern class. Choosing $k$ to minimize $\sum (k x_i - g_i)^2$ gives, by setting the derivative to zero, $k = \sum x_i g_i / \sum x_i^2$. It is least squares through the origin, a one-parameter linear regression. With five nets totalling $\sum x_i g_i = 294.03$ and $\sum x_i^2 = 300.99$, $k = 0.9769$, a 2.3% downward correction. Real calibration fits several coefficients per pattern (for example separate area, fringe and coupling terms) by linear least squares in the same way, using the normal equations or a QR factorization. A fit that minimizes relative rather than absolute error weights small nets more heavily, which suits timing better when small nets matter.

## Residual error after calibration

After applying $k$, recompute the errors. A single factor removes systematic bias but cannot remove scatter that varies from net to net. For four nets with fast values 11.1, 7.3, 7.2 and 5.4 fF against golden 10.77, 7.15, 7.34 and 5.4 fF, the fitted $k = 0.9854$ leaves a worst error of 3.34%, on the third net, which was low before calibration and is lower now. Residual scatter of this kind points to a pattern the library models poorly, and the fix is a new or finer pattern, not a different factor. Calibration must also be validated on nets not used in the fit; a factor that only matches its own training nets has been overfitted and will mislead the timer on the rest of the chip.

## Going deeper

label: Loop and partial inductance
lesson:
# Loop and partial inductance

Inductance belongs to a current loop, not to a wire, so it depends on where the return current flows. On a chip that return path is a mesh of power and ground wires that is rarely known in advance. Extractors solve this by computing partial inductances, self and mutual, for wire segments, and leaving the loop to be formed by the circuit simulation. Understanding how partial terms combine into loop inductance is the foundation of on-chip inductance extraction.

## Partial self and mutual terms

The partial inductance method assigns each segment a partial self inductance and each pair of segments a partial mutual inductance, defined as if each segment's current returned at infinity. These quantities depend only on geometry. A loop formed by a signal segment and its return combines them with signs set by current direction: for current out on the signal and back on the return, $L_{loop} = L_s + L_r - 2M$. With $L_s = 230$ pH, $L_r = 340$ pH and $M = 50$ pH, $L_{loop} = 470$ pH. The mutual term subtracts because opposing currents cancel each other's field between them. This decomposition lets an extractor emit a netlist of partial inductors and couplings without choosing the return path.

## Where the return current flows

At low frequency, return current divides by resistance. At high frequency, impedance is dominated by inductance and the current takes the path that minimizes loop inductance, which is the path closest to the signal, because a closer return has a larger mutual term. With a signal of 770 pH and two candidate returns of 710 pH each, an adjacent ground wire with $M = 550$ pH gives $770 + 710 - 1100 = 380$ pH, while a distant strap with $M = 120$ pH gives 1240 pH. Fast edges therefore concentrate return current in the nearest ground wire. This is why clock and high-speed nets are routed with dedicated shields or adjacent ground lines: they define the return path and keep loop inductance small and predictable.

## Non-additivity and dense matrices

Partial inductance does not add over length. A straight wire split into two collinear segments in series has $L = L_a + L_b + 2M_{ab}$, where $M_{ab}$ is the mutual between the halves. Segments of 620 and 230 pH with a 50 pH mutual give 950 pH, not 850. Mutual inductance between segments falls off slowly with distance, roughly logarithmically, unlike capacitive coupling, which is screened by neighbours. Every segment couples to every other, so the partial inductance matrix is dense. Extractors sparsify it with techniques such as shift-truncation, return-limited models or the inverse-inductance (susceptance) matrix, which is much more local, while preserving passivity of the resulting model.

## Going deeper

Ruehli, "Inductance calculations in a complex integrated circuit environment", IBM Journal of Research and Development (1972); Paul, "Inductance: Loop and Partial" (2010).

prereqs: Transmission lines and the telegrapher's equations
lesson:
# When on-chip inductance matters

Most on-chip nets are resistive enough that an RC model is accurate. Inductance matters on wide, low-resistance wires carrying fast edges: global clocks, wide buses and power distribution. Because full inductance extraction is expensive, flows use screening rules to decide which nets need it. These rules compare inductive and resistive impedance at the signal's significant frequency, and the signal's rise time with the wire's time of flight.

## The knee frequency

A digital edge with 10 to 90 percent rise time $t_r$ has most of its spectral energy below the knee frequency $f \approx 0.35/t_r$. This is the frequency at which to judge whether inductance matters. A clock edge of 170 ps has $f \approx 0.35/170\text{ ps} = 2.06$ GHz; a 25 ps edge has 14 GHz. The rule follows from the bandwidth of a single-pole system, whose rise time and 3 dB bandwidth satisfy $t_r f_{3dB} \approx 0.35$. Faster edges, not higher clock frequencies, are what bring inductance into play: a slow-clocked chip with sharp drivers still needs inductance analysis on its widest wires.

## Inductive versus resistive impedance

Compare $\omega L$ with $R$ at the knee frequency. If $\omega L \ll R$, the wire is resistance-dominated and RC suffices. For a 1500 um global wire with 0.2 ohm/um and 0.6 pH/um, and a 50 ps edge, $f = 7$ GHz, $\omega L = 2\pi \times 7 \times 10^9 \times 900 \times 10^{-12} = 39.6$ ohm against $R = 300$ ohm. The ratio is 0.13, so this wire is RC. The same length of a very wide top-metal wire with 0.01 ohm/um gives $R = 15$ ohm and a ratio of 2.6: inductive. Thin local wires have resistance of ohms per micron and are always RC. The loop inductance here assumes a known return path, so the screen is an estimate, used to decide where to spend accurate extraction.

## Time of flight and damping

A wire behaves as a transmission line when its signal changes faster than a wave crosses it. The time of flight is $t_f = l\sqrt{L'C'}$ for per-length inductance $L'$ and capacitance $C'$. With $L' = 0.5$ pH/um and $C' = 0.3$ fF/um, $\sqrt{L'C'} = 0.0122$ ps/um, so a 2500 um wire has $t_f = 30.6$ ps. A common screen flags the wire for an RLC model when $t_r$ is shorter than about $2t_f$ and its total resistance is below about $2Z_0$, where $Z_0 = \sqrt{L'/C'}$; here $Z_0 = 40.8$ ohm. A wire with more resistance than that is overdamped and shows no ringing. Both conditions together identify the nets where inductance changes delay and overshoot enough to matter.

## Going deeper

label: SPEF
lesson:
# SPEF

The Standard Parasitic Exchange Format (SPEF, IEEE 1481) is how an extractor hands parasitics to timers, signal-integrity tools and power analysis. It is an electrical netlist of resistors, capacitors and optionally inductors per net, with a header of units and a name map. A tool designer must know exactly what it records, because anything it does not record, such as geometry, is lost to every downstream tool, and anything it records ambiguously becomes an integration bug.

## The structure of a D_NET

A SPEF file opens with a header (`*SPEF`, design name, divider and delimiter characters, and the units `*T_UNIT`, `*C_UNIT`, `*R_UNIT`, `*L_UNIT`), then an optional `*NAME_MAP` and `*PORTS`, then one section per net. A detailed net section starts with `*D_NET name total_cap`. Its `*CONN` part lists the connection points: ports as `*P` entries and instance pins as `*I` entries, each with a direction (I, O or B). Its `*CAP` part lists capacitors: an entry with one node is a capacitor to ground, an entry with two nodes, one of them on another net, is a coupling capacitor. Its `*RES` part lists resistors between nodes. Internal nodes are named net, delimiter, index, for example n17:3. The section ends with `*END`. Every value is a bare number scaled by the header units.

## The header total

The number on the `*D_NET` line is the net's total capacitance: the sum of every entry in its `*CAP` section, ground and coupling alike. If the CAP section of n55 holds ground capacitors of 2.6, 2 and 1.7 fF and couplings of 0.9, 0.1 and 0.4 fF, the header carries 7.7 fF. Tools use the header as a quick load value and as a consistency check: a mismatch with the sum of entries signals a truncated or corrupted file. Reduced forms exist too. A `*R_NET` section carries a reduced model, and a net may be given only as a lumped total. The more a net is reduced, the less a timer can compute about its wire delay and slew to each sink.

## What SPEF does and does not carry

SPEF is per corner: resistances and capacitances depend on process and temperature, so a flow writes one file per extraction corner. It carries electrical elements, not geometry: wire layers and shapes are gone, apart from optional node coordinates, so no tool can re-extract from it. It annotates by name, so the netlist the timer loads must match the names the extractor saw; after an ECO that renames hierarchy, unmatched nets silently fall back to estimates. Coupling capacitors may be written from either net's side or both, so a reader building a coupled network must instantiate each physical capacitor once. And a writer that grounds couplings to save space keeps totals right but disables crosstalk analysis. DSPF, a SPICE-like detailed format, serves transistor-level simulation where SPEF serves STA and SI.

## Going deeper

label: Reading a SPEF net section
prereqs: Elmore delay of an RC tree
lesson:
# Reading a SPEF net section

Reading SPEF fluently means predicting its contents from a net's topology and computing timing quantities directly from its entries. Counting entries checks a writer or a reducer; totalling capacitance checks the header; and walking the resistor tree with the units in the header yields an Elmore delay. These are exactly the operations a parasitic reader and a delay calculator perform, and doing them by hand catches unit and topology mistakes that otherwise surface as baffling timing results.

## Counting entries from topology

A net whose resistor network is a tree on $p$ pins and $m$ internal nodes has $p + m$ nodes and therefore $p + m - 1$ resistors in its `*RES` section, since a tree has one fewer edge than nodes. If the extractor puts one ground capacitor on every internal node and none on pins, and the net has $c$ couplings, the `*CAP` section has $m + c$ entries. The `*CONN` section lists only the $p$ connection points. For one driver, one sink and five internal nodes, RES has 6 entries; with no couplings CAP has 5; CONN has 2. Meshes, created by multiple routes or loops, add resistors beyond the tree count, and a reader must handle them, because Elmore formulas assume a tree.

## Totals and units

Header units scale every value. With `*C_UNIT 1 FF`, a CAP section listing 1.3, 0.8 and 1.4 fF to ground and couplings of 0.3, 0.4 and 0.9 fF totals 5.1 fF. With `*C_UNIT 1 PF`, the same physical values appear as 0.0013, 0.0008 and so on, and the reader must multiply by 1000 to get femtofarads. Unit mistakes are a thousandfold error, large enough to be obvious in a delay, but a mix of files with different units in one flow can hide them in averages. A robust reader converts everything to internal units at parse time and never carries file units further, and a robust test compares the parsed totals against the header line for every net.

## Elmore delay from the entries

With `*R_UNIT 1 KOHM` and `*C_UNIT 1 FF`, resistance times capacitance comes out directly in picoseconds. For a chain driven by u1:Z through nodes n93:1, n93:2, n93:3 to sink u2:A, with resistors 0.13, 0.16, 0.03 and 0.07 kohm and capacitors 3.6, 0.8, 4 and 3.8 fF on the downstream nodes, the Elmore delay to the sink sums each resistor times all capacitance downstream of it: $0.13 \times 12.2 + 0.16 \times 8.6 + 0.03 \times 7.8 + 0.07 \times 3.8 = 3.462$ ps. Coupling capacitors are treated as grounded for this, the Miller factor 1 case. A delay calculator does this walk once per net and sink, in time linear in the number of resistors, by accumulating downstream capacitance in a reverse topological pass.

## Going deeper

IEEE Std 1481 (SPEF); Elmore, "The transient response of damped linear networks with particular regard to wideband amplifiers", Journal of Applied Physics (1948).

label: SPEF name maps and file size
lesson:
# SPEF name maps and file size

Full-chip SPEF files run to tens of gigabytes, and most of their bytes are names: long hierarchical instance and net names repeated in every entry. The name map writes each name once and refers to it by a short index token. The arithmetic of that saving explains why name maps are universal, and the same reasoning about repeated strings guides the design of every large EDA exchange format.

## Bytes saved per net

With a name map, each reference to a name of length $\ell$ is replaced by a token of length $d$ (an asterisk and digits, such as *4721), saving $\ell - d$ bytes per reference. The map itself costs one line per name: the token, a space, the name and a newline, $d + \ell + 2$ bytes. A net referenced $r$ times saves $r(\ell - d) - (d + \ell + 2)$. For $\ell = 57$, $d = 7$ and $r = 13$, the saving is $13 \times 50 - 66 = 584$ bytes. References are frequent: the D_NET line, every internal node name such as net:3, and every coupling entry on another net that touches this one all repeat the name.

## Scaling to a whole chip

Multiply the per-net saving by the net count. With 2 million nets of 31-character names, 7-character tokens and 16 references each, every net saves $16 \times 24 - 40 = 344$ bytes, so the map removes 688 MB. Parsing benefits as much as disk: a reader hashes each long name once while loading the map and afterwards works with integer indices, so lookup and memory are both cheaper. The same idea appears elsewhere, in string tables of netlist databases and in DEF and Verilog readers that intern names, and a tool designer applies it whenever a format repeats large keys.

## The break-even point

A map entry pays for itself once $r(\ell - d) > \ell + d + 2$, that is $r > (\ell + d + 2)/(\ell - d)$. For $\ell = 74$ and $d = 4$, $r > 80/70 = 1.14$, so two references suffice. Because every net in a detailed SPEF is named on its D_NET line and in each internal node name, almost every net clears the bar, and writers simply map every name. The exceptions are short names, where $\ell$ is close to $d$; once indices reach many digits, very short names can cost more mapped than unmapped, and a writer can choose to leave them inline. This is the same per-entry cost-benefit test as any dictionary compression scheme.

## Going deeper

Model order reduction by Krylov projection
lesson:
# RC network reduction

A detailed extraction can produce tens of millions of RC nodes, far more than a timer needs. RC reduction replaces each net's network with a much smaller one that behaves the same at the pins: same total capacitance, same Elmore delay to each sink, and ideally the same higher moments. Reduction sits between extraction and analysis, and its choices (what to preserve, how aggressively to eliminate, how to keep the model passive) decide whether the timer is both fast and right.

## Why reduce

Delay calculation, crosstalk analysis and power analysis all run per net, with cost growing in the number of nodes. A detailed network from fracturing has a node at every segment boundary, most of which add accuracy no analysis can use: two nodes 0.1 um apart on a wire settle almost simultaneously. Reduction keeps the port behaviour, the response seen at the driver and sinks, while removing internal nodes. The minimum requirements are that the total capacitance (the driver's load) and the first moment, or Elmore delay, to each sink are preserved. Deleting small capacitors is not reduction: it changes both. Real reduction moves charge storage and resistance onto the nodes that remain.

## Choosing the reduced model

Consider a chain: driver, $R_1 = 250$ ohm, node n1 with $C_1 = 2$ fF, $R_2 = 400$ ohm, sink with $C_2 = 3$ fF. The Elmore delay at the sink is $250 \times 5 + 400 \times 3 = 2450$ ohm-fF. Eliminating n1 leaves one 650 ohm resistor and two capacitors, one at the driver end and one at the sink. Splitting $C_1$ in proportion to the conductances of the removed resistors puts $C_1 R_2/(R_1 + R_2) = 1.23$ fF at the driver end and $C_1 R_1/(R_1+R_2) = 0.77$ fF at the sink, so the sink sees $650 \times 3.77 = 2450$ ohm-fF: preserved. Moving all of $C_1$ to the sink overestimates; dropping it loses load; splitting it in half is right only when $R_1 = R_2$.

## Accuracy, passivity and locality

Preserving only the first moment keeps Elmore delay but can distort slew and the 50% delay of resistively shielded nets, which depend on higher moments. Two families of method address this. Node elimination, such as TICER, removes nodes one at a time by a star-mesh transform, choosing nodes whose time constant is small compared with signal transitions; it is local, keeps a physical RC netlist, and suits incremental updates after an ECO. Krylov projection, such as PRIMA, projects the whole network onto a small subspace that matches several moments and is guaranteed passive, which matters because a non-passive model can generate energy and destabilize simulation. Both must treat coupling capacitors like ground capacitors during redistribution, keeping their far terminals on the aggressors.

## Going deeper

# Moments of an RC tree

The moments of a network's impulse response are the coefficients of its transfer function's Taylor expansion in $s$. The first moment is the Elmore delay; the second carries information about spread and shape. Reduction methods match moments, delay metrics are built from them, and for RC trees they have a simple path-tracing formula that a tool can evaluate in linear time.

## The first moment

Expand the transfer function from the driver to node $i$ as $H_i(s) = 1 - m_1(i) s + m_2(i) s^2 - \dots$. For an RC tree, $m_1(i) = \sum_k R_{ik} C_k$, where $R_{ik}$ is the resistance shared by the paths from the root to $i$ and to $k$, and the sum runs over every capacitor. This is the Elmore delay, the mean of the impulse response when it is nonnegative, as it is for RC trees. In a tree with 0.2 kohm from the driver to node 1 (10 fF), 0.5 kohm from node 1 to node 2 (3 fF), 0.1 kohm from node 1 to node 3 (5 fF), and 0.3 kohm from node 2 to node 4 (3 fF), node 2 shares 0.2 kohm with everything and 0.7 kohm with itself and node 4: $m_1(2) = 0.2 \times 21 + 0.5 \times 6 = 7.2$ ps.

## The second moment

Higher moments follow the same pattern recursively: $m_q(i) = \sum_k R_{ik} C_k m_{q-1}(k)$, with $m_0 = 1$. Each capacitor's contribution is weighted by its own previous moment, so the second moment needs the first moments of every node first. For a chain with 0.5 kohm to node 1 (5 fF) and 0.4 kohm to node 2 (3 fF), the first moments are $m_1(1) = 0.5 \times 8 = 4$ ps and $m_1(2) = 4 + 0.4 \times 3 = 5.2$ ps. Then $m_2(2) = 0.5 \times 5 \times 4 + 0.9 \times 3 \times 5.2 = 10 + 14.04 = 24.04$ ps$^2$. Computing all moments to order $q$ takes $q$ passes over the tree, each linear in its size, by accumulating downstream weighted capacitance.

## Why lumping fails

Moments make the cost of crude models precise. Lumping a chain into one resistor $R_{tot}$ and one capacitor $C_{tot}$ gives first moment $R_{tot} C_{tot}$, which puts every capacitor behind all the resistance. For a chain of 0.1, 0.5 and 0.4 kohm with 3, 5 and 10 fF, the true $m_1$ at the end is $0.1 \times 18 + 0.5 \times 15 + 0.4 \times 10 = 13.3$ ps, while the lump gives $1 \times 18 = 18$ ps, 35% high. A distributed uniform line has $m_1 = RC/2$, half the lump. Delay metrics such as the D2M metric combine the first two moments to approximate the 50% delay better than Elmore alone, which is an upper bound on the 50% delay of an RC tree's step response.

## Going deeper

Rubinstein, Penfield and Horowitz, "Signal delay in RC tree networks", IEEE Transactions on CAD (1983); Alpert, Devgan and Kashyap, "RC delay metrics for performance optimization", IEEE Transactions on CAD (2001).

# Node elimination by star-mesh transform

The workhorse of local RC reduction is eliminating one internal node at a time. Removing a node is Gaussian elimination on the network's nodal equations, which for a resistive star becomes the star-mesh transform: new resistors between every pair of former neighbours. The eliminated node's capacitance is spread onto those neighbours. TICER-style reducers apply this to the nodes that settle fastest, and their cost and fill-in behave exactly like sparse matrix elimination.

## The star-mesh resistors

A node $x$ connected to neighbours by conductances $g_1, \dots, g_k$, with no other path, can be eliminated exactly at DC. Solving its KCL equation for its voltage and substituting gives new conductances $g_{ij} = g_i g_j / \sum_m g_m$ between every pair of neighbours, or in resistances $R_{ij} = R_i R_j \sum_m (1/R_m)$. For three resistors of 70, 80 and 180 ohm, $\sum 1/R = 0.03234$ S, so the new resistor between the 70 and 180 ohm neighbours is $70 \times 180 \times 0.03234 = 407.5$ ohm. With two neighbours the formula reduces to the series sum $R_1 + R_2$. The transform is the Schur complement of the node's row and column in the conductance matrix.

## Redistributing the capacitance

The eliminated node's capacitance cannot simply vanish. TICER moves it to the neighbours in proportion to their conductances: neighbour $i$ receives $C_x g_i/\sum_m g_m$. With 7 fF at a node connected through 90, 140 and 80 ohm, the 90 ohm neighbour's share is $(1/90)/0.03075 = 0.361$, so it gains 2.53 fF. The shares sum to one, so total capacitance is preserved exactly, and, as the chain case shows, this split also preserves the Elmore delay at downstream nodes. It is a first-order approximation for nodes with significant capacitance; that is why only nodes with small time constants are eliminated.

## Which nodes to eliminate

A node's time constant is $\tau = C_x / \sum_m g_m$, its capacitance times the parallel resistance of its connections. A node with $\tau$ much smaller than the signal transitions tracks its neighbours almost instantly, so eliminating it barely changes waveforms. TICER marks nodes below a threshold and eliminates them; nodes with large $\tau$ shape the response and stay. For 10 fF with 1900 and 900 ohm in parallel, $\tau = 10 \times 611 = 6.1$ ps; for 5.5 fF with 100 and 1100 ohm, $\tau = 0.5$ ps. Order matters for cost: eliminating a node of degree $k$ creates up to $k(k-1)/2$ resistors, so reducers prefer low-degree nodes, exactly the minimum-degree heuristic of sparse LU, to avoid fill-in that would make the reduced network denser than the original.

## Going deeper

Sheehan, "TICER: realizable reduction of extracted RC circuits", ICCAD (1999); Davis, "Direct Methods for Sparse Linear Systems" (2006), on elimination orderings.

lesson:
# Elmore-preserving elimination in an RC chain

The conductance-proportional split of an eliminated node's capacitance is not just a heuristic: on an RC chain it preserves the Elmore delay at every downstream node exactly. Working the algebra on a small chain shows why, quantifies how badly naive lumping fails, and gives a reducer designer a concrete invariant to test against.

## Splitting the eliminated capacitance

Take a chain: driver, $R_1$, node n1 with $C_1$, $R_2$, node n2 with $C_2$, and possibly more downstream. Eliminating n1 replaces $R_1$ and $R_2$ with one resistor $R_1 + R_2$. The conductances of the removed resistors are $1/R_1$ and $1/R_2$, so the share of $C_1$ moved to n2 is $(1/R_2)/(1/R_1 + 1/R_2) = R_1/(R_1 + R_2)$ and the share moved to the driver end is $R_2/(R_1+R_2)$. With $R_1 = 0.6$ kohm, $R_2 = 0.8$ kohm and $C_1 = 2$ fF, n2 gains $2 \times 0.6/1.4 = 0.857$ fF and the driver end gets 1.143 fF. The node closer through lower resistance gets the larger share, which matches intuition: n1's voltage tracks the neighbour it is more tightly tied to.

## The Elmore delay is unchanged

Before elimination the Elmore delay at n2 (with downstream capacitance $C_d$ beyond it) is $R_1(C_1 + C_2 + C_d) + R_2(C_2 + C_d)$. After it, the single resistor $R_1 + R_2$ charges n2's new capacitance plus everything downstream: $(R_1 + R_2)(C_2 + C_d + C_1 R_1/(R_1 + R_2)) = R_1 C_1 + (R_1 + R_2)(C_2 + C_d)$, identical. The capacitance placed at the driver end is behind no resistance, so it adds load but no wire delay. For $R_1 = 0.7$, $R_2 = 0.5$ kohm, $C_1 = 11$, $C_2 = 12$ fF, the delay is $0.7 \times 23 + 0.5 \times 12 = 22.1$ ps before and after. Total capacitance is also preserved, since the two shares sum to $C_1$. These two equalities are the invariants a reducer's tests should assert on every net.

## The cost of naive lumping

A naive reducer moves all of $C_1$ onto n2. Then $C_1$ sits behind $R_1 + R_2$ instead of behind $R_1$ alone, adding $R_2 C_1$ of delay that does not exist at n2 and every node beyond. With $R_2 = 0.4$ kohm and $C_1 = 11$ fF the error is 4.4 ps on a net whose true delay is 20.8 ps, about 21%. Dropping $C_1$ instead underestimates both delay and driver load. The conductance split is exact only for the first moment; higher moments, which affect slew, change slightly, and the error grows with $C_1$'s time constant. That is why elimination is restricted to fast nodes, and why a reducer's regression suite compares slews as well as delays against the unreduced network.

## Going deeper

Sheehan, "TICER: realizable reduction of extracted RC circuits", ICCAD (1999); Rubinstein, Penfield and Horowitz, "Signal delay in RC tree networks", IEEE Transactions on CAD (1983).

label: The moment-matched pi model
lesson:
# The moment-matched pi model

A cell's delay depends on its load, but a resistive wire shields the driver from the far capacitance, so the total capacitance overstates the load. Delay calculators replace each net, as seen from its driver, with a three-element pi model, near capacitance, resistance and far capacitance, chosen to match the first three moments of the driving-point admittance. This O'Brien-Savarino model is the input to effective-capacitance computation in practically every static timer.

## The uniform line

The driving-point admittance of an RC load expands as $Y(s) = y_1 s + y_2 s^2 + y_3 s^3 + \dots$. A pi model, $C_{near}$ at the driver, then $R_\pi$, then $C_{far}$, matches the first three terms when $C_{far} = y_2^2/y_3$, $C_{near} = y_1 - C_{far}$ and $R_\pi = -y_3^2/y_2^3$. For a uniform distributed line of total $R$ and $C$, $y_1 = C$, $y_2 = -RC^2/3$ and $y_3 = 2R^2C^3/15$, which gives $C_{far} = 5C/6$, $C_{near} = C/6$ and $R_\pi = 12R/25$. A line of 1250 ohm and 18 fF becomes 3 fF, 600 ohm and 15 fF. Note that $y_1$ is always the total capacitance, so the model keeps the driver's DC load right while moving most of it behind the resistance.

## Admittance moments of a chain

For a lumped chain, compute $Y(s)$ from the far end. A capacitor alone has $Y = sC$. Behind a resistor $R$, a load $Y$ becomes $Y/(1 + RY)$, expanded as a power series; then add the capacitance at the new node. For a driver pin with 9 fF, 0.1 kohm to node 1 with 15 fF, and 0.1 kohm to node 2 with 12 fF, this gives $y_1 = 36$ fF, $y_2 = -87.3$ kohm fF$^2$ and $y_3 = 291.87$ kohm$^2$ fF$^3$. Then $C_{far} = 87.3^2/291.87 = 26.11$ fF and $C_{near} = 9.89$ fF. With small resistances most capacitance stays visible to the driver: $C_{far}$ here sits behind only a small $R_\pi$. The recursion is linear in the tree size, and branches simply add admittances at their junction.

## The resistance and its use

The pi resistance is $R_\pi = -y_3^2/y_2^3$, positive because $y_2$ is negative. For a chain with 8 fF at the pin, 0.8 kohm to 20 fF and 0.5 kohm to 16 fF, the moments give $R_\pi = 0.926$ kohm, $C_{near} = 8.54$ fF and $C_{far} = 35.46$ fF. The delay calculator then finds an effective capacitance: the single capacitance that draws the same charge from the driver as the pi load during the driver's transition. A slow driver sees nearly all 44 fF; a fast one sees little more than $C_{near}$. The effective capacitance indexes the Liberty table for the cell delay, and the pi model, or the full reduced network, is then used again to compute the wire delay from driver to each sink.

label: The Miller factor of a coupling capacitor
lesson:
# The Miller factor of a coupling capacitor

A coupling capacitor's effect on its victim depends on what the other end does. If the neighbour is quiet, the capacitor acts like one to ground. If the neighbour switches the opposite way, the voltage across the capacitor changes twice as much and the victim's driver must supply twice the charge. If it switches the same way, the capacitor carries no charge. The Miller factor, 0, 1 or 2, captures this in a single multiplier, and it is the basis of every switching-aware delay calculation.

## Effective coupling

The current through a capacitor is $C\, d(V_v - V_a)/dt$, where $V_v$ and $V_a$ are the victim and aggressor voltages. When the victim swings by $\Delta V$ and the aggressor is quiet, the change across the capacitor is $\Delta V$: it behaves like $C_c$ to ground, Miller factor 1. If the aggressor swings by $-\Delta V$ at the same time, the change is $2\Delta V$, so the capacitor looks like $2C_c$ to ground, Miller factor 2. If the aggressor swings by $+\Delta V$ simultaneously, the change is zero and the capacitor looks like nothing, Miller factor 0. A 2.2 fF coupling therefore contributes 0, 2.2 or 4.4 fF of effective load depending on the neighbour. Timers replace each coupling with a grounded capacitor of $k C_c$ for the chosen factor $k$.

## Charge through the coupling

The factor is a statement about charge. During the transition the victim's driver pushes $Q = C_c \Delta(V_v - V_a)$ through the coupling capacitor. For a victim rising 0.8 V with an aggressor falling 0.8 V through 5.3 fF, the change across the capacitor is 1.6 V and the charge is 8.48 fC, the same as a 10.6 fF grounded capacitor would draw. With the aggressor quiet the charge is 4.24 fC, and with it rising alongside, zero. The values 0 and 2 assume simultaneous transitions of equal slew; real aggressors switch with different slews and offsets, so the effective factor can lie between the extremes, and some analyses use factors outside 0 to 2 for very different slews. Signoff tools compute the coupling current from waveforms rather than trusting a fixed factor.

## Bounding with unknown aggressors

Without timing information about the aggressors, a timer must bound. Max-delay (setup) analysis assumes every aggressor switches against the victim, factor 2. Min-delay (hold) analysis assumes every aggressor switches with it, factor 0. The difference in effective coupling between the two analyses is $2\sum C_c$; for couplings of 2.5 and 3.5 fF that is 12 fF. That spread is the pessimism of not knowing the aggressors' timing, and on a net whose capacitance is mostly coupling it can double the delay range. Timing windows, logical correlation (two nets that cannot switch in opposite directions) and aggressor filtering by size all exist to shrink it.

## Going deeper

label: Switching-dependent effective capacitance
prereqs: The Miller factor of a coupling capacitor
lesson:
# Switching-dependent effective capacitance

Once each coupling has a Miller factor, a victim's effective load is its ground and pin capacitance plus every coupling scaled by its factor. That number goes straight into the delay calculation, and it changes with the aggressors' behaviour. Computing it for specific scenarios, and its worst and best cases, shows how much of a net's timing is decided by its neighbours rather than by its own driver and wire.

## A specific switching scenario

For a victim with ground capacitance $C_g$, pin capacitance $C_p$ and couplings $C_{c,i}$ with factors $k_i$, the effective load is $C_{eff} = C_g + C_p + \sum_i k_i C_{c,i}$. A victim with 3.7 fF of wire to ground and 4 fF of pins, with three aggressors of 0.8, 3.6 and 2.8 fF all switching against it, sees $3.7 + 4 + 2 \times 7.2 = 22.1$ fF. Had they all been quiet, it would see 14.9 fF. The coupling elements must be in the parasitic netlist with their aggressor identities for this to be possible; a grounded-coupling SPEF only supports the quiet case. In tools, the scenario comes from timing windows and switching directions computed by the timer.

## The worst case

For setup analysis without window information, the worst case sets every factor to 2: $C_{eff,max} = C_g + C_p + 2\sum C_{c,i}$. A victim with 10.8 fF to ground, 3.9 fF of pins and couplings of 0.6, 1.3 and 0.5 fF has $C_{eff,max} = 14.7 + 4.8 = 19.5$ fF. Note that this goes beyond the extracted total capacitance of 17.1 fF: the effective load is not bounded by the physical capacitance. Small couplings are often filtered out below a threshold, either grounded or ignored as aggressors, to keep analysis tractable; the filter must be applied carefully, because a hundred small couplings to one bus can add up to a large one.

## The spread between cases

The best case for delay, factor 0 on every coupling, leaves $C_g + C_p$. The ratio of worst to best is $1 + 2\sum C_c / (C_g + C_p)$. For 11.3 fF to ground, 3.3 fF of pins and 7 fF of coupling, it is $28.6/14.6 = 1.96$: the victim's delay could nearly double between scenarios. That spread is why crosstalk is a signoff check of its own. It also tells a router where to act: a net whose coupling is a large share of its capacitance gains most from extra spacing or shielding, and a net whose capacitance is mostly ground and pins gains little.

## Going deeper

label: Crosstalk-induced delay
prereqs: Elmore delay of an RC tree
lesson:
# Crosstalk-induced delay

When an aggressor switches during a victim's transition, the victim's delay changes: slower if the aggressor opposes it, faster if it helps. The change is crosstalk-induced delay, or delta delay. Setup analysis must use the slow-down and hold analysis the speed-up, so crosstalk can break both checks. Computing delta delay with a simple driver model connects the Miller factor to slack and shows why SI analysis is part of every signoff timing run.

## Delay with a quiet aggressor

Model the victim's driver as a resistance $R_d$ charging a lumped load, with 50% delay $t = 0.69 R_d C$; with kohm and fF the result is in ps. With a quiet aggressor, coupling counts at face value, so $C = C_g + C_c$. A 3.2 kohm driver with 4.5 fF to ground (including pins) and 2.7 fF of coupling has $t = 0.69 \times 3.2 \times 7.2 = 15.9$ ps. This quiet case is what a timer without SI reports when it grounds the couplings. Real delay calculators use effective-capacitance iteration and the reduced RC network instead of a lumped load, but the dependence of delay on the coupling's effective value is the same, and the lumped model keeps the arithmetic transparent.

## The delta delay

When the aggressor opposes the victim, the factor rises from 1 to 2 and the effective load grows by $C_c$; the delay grows by $\Delta t = 0.69 R_d C_c$. When it switches the same way, the factor falls to 0, and the delay falls by the same amount. A 2.4 kohm driver with 2.6 fF of coupling has $\Delta t = 0.69 \times 2.4 \times 2.6 = 4.31$ ps in either direction. The delta is proportional to the driver's resistance: weak drivers on long, coupled nets are the usual victims. Upsizing the victim's driver shrinks the delta; so do spacing, shielding and moving the net to another layer. Delta delay also changes the victim's output slew, which propagates to downstream stages.

## Effect on setup and hold

Setup slack uses the latest arrival, so it takes the slow-down; hold slack uses the earliest arrival, so it takes the speed-up. A hold check with 31 ps of slack through a victim with a 1.7 kohm driver and 3.1 fF of coupling loses $0.69 \times 1.7 \times 3.1 = 3.64$ ps when the aggressor can switch with it, leaving 27.36 ps. A setup path with 5 ps of slack and a 6 ps slow-down fails. Signoff timing therefore runs SI-aware analysis for both checks, with delta delays computed per arc. Because delta delay depends on when aggressors switch, and their switching depends on the delays, the analysis iterates timing windows until they converge, and every ECO that moves wires reopens it.

## Going deeper

Sapatnekar, "Timing" (2004), the chapter on crosstalk-aware timing; Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter on timing closure.

label: Crosstalk glitches
lesson:
# Crosstalk glitches

A quiet net is not safe from its neighbours. When an aggressor switches, charge injected through the coupling capacitor bumps the victim's voltage, a glitch. If the glitch is large enough and reaches a sequential element or a dynamic node, it can flip a stored value, a functional failure rather than a timing one. The first estimate of a glitch's size is a capacitive divider, an upper bound that every noise analysis starts from.

## The capacitive divider

Suppose the victim's driver is too weak to respond during a fast aggressor edge, so the victim floats. The aggressor's swing $V_{DD}$ divides across the coupling and the victim's other capacitance: $V_p = V_{DD}\, C_c/(C_c + C_g)$, by charge conservation on the floating node. A victim with 7.9 fF to ground and 1.4 fF of coupling to a 1 V aggressor sees $1.4/9.3 = 150.5$ mV. Real victims are held by a driver that bleeds the injected charge away, so the real peak is lower; the divider is the bound, reached when the aggressor edge is much faster than the victim's holding time constant. Static noise analysis uses it as a cheap filter: nets whose bound is below the noise threshold need no further work.

## Several aggressors

With several aggressors, every coupling is part of the divider's total. Switching aggressors push charge in; quiet ones act as ground. If aggressor A (1.5 fF) rises while B (2 fF) stays quiet on a victim with 7 fF to ground, $V_p = 1.5/(1.5 + 2 + 7) = 142.9$ mV, lower than if B were not there, because B's coupling loads the victim. If both rise together, the switching coupling is 3.5 fF and $V_p = 3.5/10.5$ of the swing. Glitch analysis therefore needs to know which aggressors can switch in the same direction at the same time, which comes from timing windows and logic; assuming all aggressors align is pessimistic but safe.

## Shielding

Inserting a grounded shield wire between victim and aggressor converts much of the coupling into capacitance to the shield, which is ground. The victim's total capacitance stays about the same, but the switching coupling drops. For a victim with 7.2 fF to ground and 1.6 fF of coupling to a 1 V aggressor, the bound is 181.8 mV; if a shield converts 60% of the coupling, the remaining 0.64 fF gives 72.7 mV, a 109 mV improvement. Shielding costs a routing track and adds ground capacitance, which slows the victim slightly. That is why it is reserved for clocks, asynchronous resets and other nets where a glitch is fatal, while ordinary nets are fixed with spacing or by upsizing the victim's holding driver.

## Going deeper
