lesson:
# Glitch peak with a holding driver and noise immunity

A real victim is not floating: its driver holds it at its rail through a finite resistance, and that resistance drains injected charge during the aggressor's edge. The glitch peak then depends on the ratio of the aggressor's rise time to the victim's time constant. Comparing that peak with what the receiving gate can tolerate, its noise immunity, is how glitch signoff decides whether a glitch is a violation.

## The holding-resistance model

Model the victim's driver as a resistance $R$ to its rail, with $C_g$ to ground and $C_c$ to an aggressor ramping from 0 to $V_{DD}$ in $t_r$. During the ramp the coupling injects a constant current $C_c V_{DD}/t_r$, and the victim obeys $(C_c + C_g)\, dv/dt + v/R = C_c V_{DD}/t_r$. Its solution rises toward $R C_c V_{DD}/t_r$ with time constant $\tau = R(C_c + C_g)$, and the peak, at the end of the ramp, is $V_p = V_{DD}\frac{R C_c}{t_r}(1 - e^{-t_r/\tau})$. For $R = 3.5$ kohm, $C_g = 2.1$ fF, $C_c = 0.8$ fF and a 0.9 V, 55 ps ramp, $\tau = 10.15$ ps and $V_p = 900 \times 0.0509 \times 0.996 = 45.6$ mV. After the ramp the victim decays back with time constant $\tau$.

## Noise margin

A glitch matters only if the receiving gate responds to it. The simplest test compares the peak with a flat threshold, a fraction of $V_{DD}$ derived from the receiver's DC noise margin, and reports the margin, threshold minus peak. For a 140.4 mV peak against a 25% threshold at 0.8 V (200 mV), the margin is 59.6 mV, a pass. Real noise-immunity curves depend on the glitch width: a pulse much shorter than the receiver's own delay is filtered and can exceed the DC threshold safely, while a wide pulse must stay below it. Glitches also propagate: a glitch that partly passes a gate can combine with others downstream, so noise analysis checks propagated noise at sequential and dynamic inputs, where a latched glitch becomes a functional failure.

## Rise time versus the bound

The ratio of the holding-driver peak to the floating bound $V_{DD} C_c/(C_c + C_g)$ is $(\tau/t_r)(1 - e^{-t_r/\tau})$, which depends only on $t_r/\tau$. For a fast aggressor ($t_r \ll \tau$) it approaches 1: the driver has no time to react. For a slow one ($t_r \gg \tau$) it approaches $\tau/t_r$: the driver bleeds charge as fast as it arrives. With $R = 3$ kohm, 1.9 fF to ground, 1.2 fF of coupling and a 20 ps edge, $\tau = 9.3$ ps and the peak is 41% of the 290 mV bound. The model tells a tool which fix works: a stronger holding driver lowers $\tau$ and the peak, slowing the aggressor lowers the peak, and reducing coupling lowers both the bound and the peak.

## Going deeper

label: Timing windows and aggressor filtering
lesson:
# Timing windows and aggressor filtering

Assuming every aggressor switches against every victim at the worst moment is safe but very pessimistic. A timer knows, for each net, the window of time in which it can switch. An aggressor whose window does not overlap the victim's cannot affect the victim's transition. Filtering aggressors by window overlap is the main tool for removing crosstalk pessimism, and it couples timing and SI into an iteration.

## Window overlap

Static timing computes, for each net, the earliest and latest times it can switch: its timing window $[e, l]$. An aggressor with window $[e_a, l_a]$ can affect a victim with window $[e_v, l_v]$ only if the intervals overlap, $e_a \le l_v$ and $l_a \ge e_v$. For a victim switching in [200, 280] ps, aggressors in [350, 400], [220, 260] and [210, 250] ps give two overlaps; the first aggressor has finished switching long before or will start long after, as far as this victim's transition is concerned. Non-overlapping aggressors are treated as quiet, Miller factor 1, rather than removed: their coupling still loads the victim. Some tools pad windows by the aggressor's slew to account for the finite transition.

## Pessimism removed

Without windows, setup analysis must assume all aggressors oppose, adding $0.69 R_d \sum C_c$ of delay over the quiet case. With windows, only overlapping aggressors count. The pessimism removed is $0.69 R_d \sum_{\text{non-overlap}} C_c$. For a 2.3 kohm victim driver with aggressors of 0.9, 2 and 0.6 fF, of which only the 0.9 fF one overlaps, the full delta is $0.69 \times 2.3 \times 3.5 = 5.55$ ps and the windowed delta is 1.43 ps: 4.13 ps of pessimism removed. On a chip with millions of coupled nets, this is often the difference between hundreds of false SI violations and a handful of real ones. Logical correlation, such as two outputs that can never switch in opposite directions, removes more.

## The windowed delta and the iteration

The reported delta delay counts only overlapping aggressors, each at factor 2: for a 1.7 kohm driver and overlapping couplings totalling 6.5 fF, $0.69 \times 1.7 \times 6.5 = 7.62$ ps. But the delta changes the victim's arrival, which moves its window, and every aggressor's window depends on its own crosstalk delays in turn. SI-aware timing therefore iterates: compute windows without crosstalk, compute deltas, recompute windows, repeat until windows stop moving. Zhou, Shenoy and Nicholls showed that this is a fixpoint computation on a lattice, which explains when and to what it converges; in practice it settles in a few rounds. An incremental timer must re-run this locally after every ECO, since moving one wire changes couplings and windows for its neighbours.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# RC corners and signoff scenarios

Interconnect varies with the process just as transistors do: metal width, thickness and dielectric height all have tolerances. Extraction captures this with RC corners, sets of extreme wire geometries, and signoff combines them with transistor corners and functional modes into scenarios. Knowing which RC corner is worst for which net, and how many scenarios result, explains both the cost of signoff and why no single corner can stand for the rest.

## Counting scenarios

A scenario is one mode (functional, test, low-power) at one PVT corner (process, voltage, temperature) with one RC corner. Setup and hold are signed off at different corners: setup at slow transistors with Cworst and RCworst wiring, hold at fast transistors with Cbest and RCbest, among others. With 2 modes, setup at 3 PVT corners each with 3 RC corners, and hold at 2 PVT corners each with 2 RC corners, there are $2 \times 3 \times 3 + 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 26$ scenarios. Extraction runs once per RC corner and is shared across the PVT corners that use it, with temperature applied to resistance. Multi-mode multi-corner timers analyse many scenarios in one run, sharing the timing graph and keeping per-scenario arrival times.

## Corner geometry

RC corners move geometry to extremes. In the Cworst corner, wires are wider and thicker and dielectrics thinner, so capacitance, especially coupling, is highest, and resistance is somewhat lower. In RCworst, wires are narrower and thinner, so resistance is highest and capacitance somewhat lower. Resistance goes as $1/(WT)$: with width 8% and thickness 10% below nominal, a 340 ohm wire becomes $340/(0.92 \times 0.9) = 410.6$ ohm, 21% higher. Corners are derived from the foundry's statistical process data at a stated sigma level, and the technology file for each corner describes the stack with those dimensions. Because width and thickness move together in a corner, these are correlated extremes, not independent worst cases.

## Which corner is worst

A net's delay is roughly $0.69[R_d(C_w + C_L) + R_w(C_w/2 + C_L)]$. The driver term depends on capacitance only, the wire term on the product. Short, driver-dominated nets are worst at Cworst; long, resistive nets can be worst at RCworst. For a 0.8 kohm driver, 2.7 kohm of wire, 36 fF of wire and 18 fF of load, Cworst (R scaled 0.95, C 1.1) gives 98.7 ps and RCworst (R 1.15, C 0.96) gives 104.6 ps: this long net is RC-limited. A design contains both kinds of net, often on the same path, so signoff runs both corners, and a path can even be worst at a mixed condition no standard corner represents, which is one motivation for statistical extraction.

## Going deeper

label: Electromigration and IR-drop signoff
lesson:
# Electromigration and IR-drop signoff

Extracted resistance feeds two reliability and power checks. Electromigration (EM) signoff checks that current densities in wires and vias are low enough for the chip to last its rated lifetime. IR-drop signoff checks that the power grid delivers voltage within budget to every cell. Both are computed from the extracted power and signal networks, and both can be broken by an innocent-looking timing ECO.

## Current density

Electromigration is the slow drift of metal atoms pushed by the electron flow, which eventually opens voids or forms shorts. Its rate depends on current density $J = I/(WT)$. A power strap 0.1 um wide and 0.2 um thick carrying 5.6 mA has $J = 5.6/0.02 = 280$ mA/um$^2$; against a limit of 200 mA/um$^2$ it fails. EM rules come from the foundry per layer, per via type and per temperature, with separate limits for DC (unidirectional, as in power nets), average, RMS and peak current on signal nets. EM signoff computes currents from the extracted network and activity, divides by the extracted cross-section, and flags violations. The fix is wider wires, more vias or less current per wire.

## IR drop along a strap

Current flowing through grid resistance drops voltage: $\Delta V = IR$. A strap with sheet resistance 0.02 ohm/sq, 2 um wide and 750 um long has 375 squares, 7.5 ohm, and delivering 5 mA through it costs 37.5 mV, 4.2% of a 0.9 V supply. Real grids are meshes of many layers, solved as large sparse linear systems (nodal analysis with current sources at cell taps), statically with average currents and dynamically with time-varying switching. Signoff budgets static plus dynamic drop at a few percent of the supply. The drop matters for timing because cells slow down at lower voltage, so signoff timers take per-instance voltages from IR analysis.

## Lifetime scaling

Black's equation models EM lifetime as $\text{MTTF} \propto J^{-n} e^{E_a/kT}$, with a current exponent $n$ typically between 1 and 2 and an activation energy $E_a$ specific to the metal and its interfaces. At a fixed temperature, raising $J$ by a factor of 2 with $n = 2$ cuts lifetime to $2^{-2} = 0.25$ of its old value. Temperature enters exponentially, so hot spots age fastest. The design consequence: a timing ECO that upsizes a driver raises the current in its output wire and the vias under it, possibly past the EM limit, even though timing improved. Every timing ECO must be followed by EM and IR re-checks, which is one of the dependencies an automated ECO loop must respect.

## Going deeper

label: The signoff checklist
lesson:
# The signoff checklist

Signoff is the set of checks a design must pass before tape-out, each run with the qualified tools at the worst conditions for what it checks. No single check covers another's failure modes: a design can meet timing and fail LVS, or pass DRC and fail in the field from electromigration. A tool designer working on any engine needs to know where its output lands in this checklist and which other checks it can silently break.

## The categories

Digital signoff covers five groups. Timing: setup and hold, with signal integrity, across all modes and corners, using signoff extraction. Power: total and per-domain power, and power-intent checks for multi-voltage designs. Reliability: electromigration on power and signal nets, and IR drop, static and dynamic. Physical verification: design-rule checking (DRC) against the foundry deck, layout versus schematic (LVS) to prove the layout implements the netlist, antenna checks for charge damage during processing, and density checks for polishing uniformity. Function: logical equivalence checking (LEC) between the final netlist and the reference, after all optimization and ECOs. Each check has its own tool and its own definition of clean, and tape-out requires all of them.

## Matching checks to conditions

Each check runs where it is hardest to pass. Setup at slow transistors, low voltage and the Cworst or RCworst wiring; hold at fast transistors, high voltage and Cbest or RCbest. Crosstalk needs coupling capacitors in the parasitics, not just totals. Timing with IR-drop awareness needs per-instance voltages from dynamic IR analysis. EM is worst at high temperature. Density matters because chemical-mechanical polishing dishes sparse regions and erodes dense ones, so fill is inserted, and that fill must be present in the final extraction because it adds capacitance. A block clean at the typical corner only has passed none of these; a missing corner is the most common signoff gap.

## The checklist after changes

Every late change re-opens the checklist. An ECO changes netlist and geometry, so timing, SI, EM/IR, DRC, LVS and LEC must all be re-run on its effects, typically incrementally. Metal fill after extraction invalidates parasitics. A change in temperature range or voltage can expose temperature inversion, where at low supply voltage cells are slowest when cold, so the slow corner moves. Signoff must also be run with the qualified extractor rather than the router's internal estimates, because only the former is calibrated to the foundry's golden solver. A disciplined flow records which version of every input each check used, so that the final signoff is provably consistent: the same netlist, the same layout and the same parasitics everywhere.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), the chapters on timing closure and physical verification; the OpenROAD flow scripts' final-report stage, which runs the open-source equivalents of these checks.

label: Engineering change orders
lesson:
# Engineering change orders

An engineering change order (ECO) is a targeted change to a nearly finished design: a logic fix found late in verification, or a timing or noise fix found at signoff. Instead of re-running synthesis and place-and-route, which would perturb everything that already closed, an ECO touches only what must change. ECOs are where extraction, timing and physical tools meet under the most time pressure, and they come in kinds with very different costs.

## Functional and timing ECOs

A functional ECO changes what the logic computes: it fixes a bug, such as an inverted enable or a wrong reset value. Equivalence checking against the corrected RTL must then pass, while equivalence against the old netlist fails in exactly the intended way. A timing ECO changes cells or wires without changing function: upsizing or downsizing a cell, swapping its threshold-voltage flavour, inserting a buffer or delay cell, or rerouting a net. It must remain logically equivalent to the pre-ECO netlist. Both are preferred to a re-run of the flow because weeks of timing, SI and physical closure elsewhere are preserved. ECO tools work at the netlist and placement level, then incrementally route, extract and re-time.

## Metal-only ECOs and spare cells

After tape-out, masks are expensive, and wafers are often held after the base (transistor) layers are processed. A metal-only ECO changes only metal and via layers, so the base masks are reused and held wafers can be finished with the new metal masks. It cannot add transistors, so designers scatter spare cells (NANDs, NORs, inverters, flip-flops, with inputs tied off) across the die before tape-out. A fix is mapped onto nearby spares and wired in. Spare flops often have their clock pins prewired so the clock tree need not change. Some flows use gate-array-style filler cells that can be configured as logic by metal alone, making more resources available.

## Side effects and re-verification

An ECO is local in intent but not in effect. A new buffer adds load to its driver and coupling to its neighbours; a rerouted wire changes the capacitance of every wire beside it; an upsized cell speeds short paths through it and can break hold. So after an ECO, extraction must cover the touched nets and their geometric neighbours, timing and SI must be re-run, and EM, IR, DRC, LVS and equivalence must be re-checked. A functional ECO is proven with formal equivalence against the corrected RTL, not by a simulation of the failing test, since only equivalence covers every input. The best ECO is the smallest change that passes all of these, which is why ECO tools search for minimal patches.

## Going deeper

# Metal-only ECOs with spare cells

A metal-only ECO is a small physical design problem with tight constraints: find spare cells of the right types close to where the fix belongs, wire them in with new metal, and change as few mask layers as possible. Each step is computable: nearest-spare search, wirelength of the new nets, and the mask count the change implies. Together they decide whether a late bug fix costs days or a respin.

## Finding the nearest spare

The fix needs particular cell types near a target point, typically the centroid of the pins it must connect. Among unused spare cells of each needed type, the router prefers the closest by Manhattan distance, $|x - x_0| + |y - y_0|$, since routing is rectilinear. If an ECO needs a NOR2 at (320, 270) um and NOR2 spares sit at (240, 160), (360, 140) and (500, 350), their distances are 190, 170 and 260 um, so the second is chosen. Spatial indexes, such as a k-d tree or a grid of bins per cell type, make this query fast on chips with many thousands of spares. A spare too far away adds wire delay that can defeat a timing fix, so spare density is a design-time trade between area and ECO reach.

## Wirelength of the new net

Once a spare is chosen, it must be wired to its sinks. Half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL), the sum of the bounding box's width and height over all pins, estimates the wire needed. A spare inverter at (360, 0) driving sinks at (110, 390), (110, 380) and (340, 260) has a bounding box 250 um wide and 390 um tall, HPWL 640 um. That wire adds resistance and capacitance, so the ECO's timing must be checked with the new net's extracted parasitics, not with the ideal delay of the inserted cell. Several fixes competing for the same spares become a small assignment problem: minimize total HPWL subject to each fix getting a cell of the right type, solvable as a bipartite matching.

## Masks changed

The cost of a metal-only ECO is the set of masks that must be remade. Every metal layer the change touches needs new masks, and so does every via layer between them. Multiple patterning multiplies this: a layer printed with double patterning has two masks. If an ECO rewires M1 through M5 with V1 through V4, and M1 to M4 are double patterned, the masks are $4 \times 2 + 1 = 9$ metal plus 4 via, 13 in total. Confining the fix to upper layers, for example using spares whose inputs are tied off on an upper layer so that reconnection only needs upper metal, cuts the mask count and cost sharply. This is why spare-cell design decides which layers carry the tie-offs.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapters on placement and routing; the OpenROAD documentation on its ECO and spare-cell commands.

lesson:
# PPA closure

Closing a design means meeting its performance target within its power and area budgets, all measured by signoff tools: PPA closure. Every fix trades one against another. Upsizing and low-Vt swaps buy speed with power; spacing and shielding buy SI margin with routing area; voltage buys everything with power and reliability. The final weeks of a project are a search over such trades, and the right choice depends on which constraint binds where.

## The trade-offs

Each closure move has a cost profile. Swapping a cell to a lower threshold voltage speeds it but multiplies its leakage, often several times. Upsizing speeds a gate but raises its input capacitance, its area and its switching power, and can slow its driver. Buffering long nets trades area and power for delay. Spacing or shielding a net reduces coupling and crosstalk without adding leakage, but consumes routing tracks. Raising the supply voltage speeds everything but raises dynamic power with the square of voltage and stresses EM and IR budgets. A design with large positive slack everywhere is not optimal: it is over-designed, and closure includes recovering power and area on non-critical paths.

## Choosing a fix

Given a failing endpoint and candidate fixes with known slack gains and costs, the closure choice is the cheapest fix that actually closes. With WNS of -40 ps and candidates of +55 ps for 0.2 uW of leakage, +30 ps for 1.7 uW, +43 ps for 0.7 uW and +49 ps for 0.7 uW, the 30 ps fix fails to close and is out, and the 55 ps upsizing at 0.2 uW is cheapest among the rest. Real optimizers solve this over many endpoints at once, with interacting fixes on shared logic, using sensitivity-guided greedy moves or Lagrangian relaxation, and they re-time incrementally after each batch. The cost function encodes the project's priorities, so it is a parameter, not a constant of the tool.

## Closure with margins

Closure is only real at signoff accuracy. Optimization often runs on fast extraction and timing; paths closed with zero margin in fast mode can reopen at signoff when the accurate extractor shifts their slack. A disciplined flow keeps margin proportional to the fast mode's error on near-critical paths, or recurses to accurate extraction for them. Power recovery spends positive slack, so it must respect a margin too, or it creates new near-critical paths. And every fix changes parasitics, which changes switching power, so power analysis must use post-ECO parasitics. The value of a trade depends on context: 4% more area in a frequency-limiting block is worth it if the die and floorplan absorb it, and worthless if they do not.

## Going deeper

Sapatnekar, "Timing" (2004), chapters on gate sizing and optimization; Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter on timing closure.

lesson:
# The extractor's core and change surface

An extractor built for an agent-first flow is split into a small immutable core and a change surface that agents and engineers can adjust without touching the core. For extraction the core is the field-solver mathematics and netlist correctness; the change surface is the accuracy-versus-speed mode, net and layer selection, the pattern library and calibration. Placing each customer request in the right layer and tier, and putting the seam where requests actually vary, is what keeps core edits rare.

## Core and change surface

The four-layer model orders an engine's parts by how hard they are to change. The immutable core of an extractor holds what makes it correct: the discretized Laplace solve and its numerical kernel, the assembly of the capacitance matrix, and netlist correctness, meaning every resistor and capacitor is attached to the right net and node. These are shared by every customer and change only with human approval and full regression. Strategy covers the pattern-matching and fracturing policies. Parameters cover the accuracy mode, the net and layer selection, thresholds for coupling filtering and calibration tables. Observation hooks expose per-net parasitic summaries, couplings by aggressor and the estimated error of the mode used, so an agent can decide what to re-extract.

## Tiers for extraction requests

Requests land in the smallest safe tier. Extracting clock nets with the 3D solver and the rest with patterns is Tier 1, a selection setting. Refitting pattern coefficients to new foundry golden data is Tier 1, a calibration table change validated against the golden results. A new cell architecture whose via-rail structure matches no existing pattern needs new recognition code at the pattern-library seam: Tier 2, a plug-in. Changing the mesh-refinement algorithm inside the 3D solver is Tier 3, a core edit with a reviewed diff and regression against every golden result. A seam is placed well when the common requests, new processes, new layout styles and new accuracy targets, are all Tier 1 or Tier 2.

## Designing the capacitance-model seam

The seam between geometry and capacitance sits at a capacitance-model interface: the core fractures geometry and builds connectivity, then asks a model for per-length ground and coupling values for each cross-section. To host table, calibrated and surrogate models alike, the seam must pass the layer, width, spacing to each neighbour and that neighbour's net, the layers above and below, local density and the corner. It must be coarse, called per batch of segments with plain arrays rather than per segment through a virtual call, so the core's hot loop stays fast. It must be deterministic: the same layout must give the same parasitics on every run, or differential checks cannot separate an ECO's effect from noise.

## Going deeper

The OpenRCX extractor in OpenROAD, whose pattern-based model files illustrate a calibration data seam; Ousterhout, "A Philosophy of Software Design" (2nd ed., 2021), on deep modules and interfaces.

lesson:
# Calibration as a Tier 1 change

Calibration is the extractor's most frequent change, and it should never require a recompile. If correction factors per pattern class live in a configuration table, a new process revision, a new fill style or new golden data becomes a Tier 1 change: fit the coefficients, validate them, promote the table. An agent can run that whole loop, provided the validation is strict enough that a bad fit cannot slip through.

## Fitting the table entry

For one pattern class, collect samples of fast-mode values $x_i$ and golden 3D-solver values $g_i$. The least-squares scale factor is $k = \sum x_i g_i / \sum x_i^2$. For four samples with $\sum x_i g_i = 124.54$ and $\sum x_i^2 = 130.82$, $k = 0.952$: fast mode reads 5% high for this class. The new $k$ is written into the configuration table for that class. Nothing in the core changes: the fracturing, the lookup and the netlist assembly are the same code, and the only artifact that changes is data. That is what makes the change Tier 1, and what lets it be versioned, reviewed as a data diff and rolled back by restoring the previous table.

## Applying the calibrated table

After the update, fast mode multiplies each extracted value of the class by its factor. With $k = 1.0215$ and an uncalibrated value of 4.7 fF, the reported value is 4.801 fF. The factor applies per class, so a net that crosses several classes gets each segment corrected by its own factor before summing. Agents and flows must record which table version produced each parasitic file, since two runs with different tables are not comparable. This matters for differential checks: a calibration change moves every net of the class, and a differential report must attribute that movement to the table change, not to an ECO run at the same time. Calibration updates and design changes should therefore never be mixed in one step.

## Validation before promotion

A fitted factor must be validated on held-out nets that were not used in the fit. Scale each held-out fast value by the new $k$, compare with golden, and count nets outside the tolerance. If six held-out nets give four beyond a 2% tolerance after scaling by 1.0068, the fit has not captured the class: the scatter is not a uniform bias, and the right response is a new or finer pattern, a Tier 2 change, not a further tweak of the factor. Promotion requires the count to be zero, or within a stated budget. This gate is what keeps a Tier 1 change safe in an agent's hands: the agent can propose and fit freely, but only a validated table reaches signoff.

## Going deeper

Kao, Lo, Basel and Singh, "Parasitic extraction: current state of the art and future trends", Proceedings of the IEEE (2001), on calibration of pattern-based extraction.

lesson:
# Fast and accurate extraction in an agent loop

An agent that optimizes a layout cannot wait for signoff extraction after every move. It runs a fast extraction mode in its inner loop and recurses to the accurate engine only where the fast answer cannot be trusted. Deciding where that is requires an error bound per net, a rule that turns bounds and slack into a re-extraction list, and an accounting of what the loop saves.

## Error bounds on fast results

A fast mode is characterized by its error against the accurate engine, for example within 10% on net capacitance across a validation set. If a net's interconnect-driven delay scales linearly with its capacitance, its delay error bound is that fraction of its delay: a 247 ps net carries a 24.7 ps bound. The bound is the honest uncertainty of the fast result, and an agent should carry it with every fast-mode slack. Bounds are better per pattern class or per net type than global: a fast mode may be within 2% on long parallel runs and 15% on dense via regions. An observation hook that reports the bound with the parasitics is what makes the fast mode usable by an agent at all.

## Which nets to recurse on

A net's fast-mode slack is ambiguous when its magnitude is within its error bound, because the true slack could have either sign. Those nets go to accurate extraction; clearly passing or clearly failing nets keep their fast values. With a 4% error and six nets of slack and delay $(-3, 30)$, $(30, 210)$, $(-10, 290)$, $(-12, 20)$, $(0, 70)$ and $(-1, 110)$ ps, the bounds are 1.2, 8.4, 11.6, 0.8, 2.8 and 4.4 ps, and the ambiguous nets are the third, fifth and sixth. This is the recursion rule of the fast-accurate loop. It is conservative in the right direction: a net is accepted on fast data only when even the worst fast-mode error could not change its verdict.

## What the loop saves

Cost decides how tight the error bound must be. With 200000 nets, fast extraction at 0.2 ms per net and accurate at 10 ms, all-accurate takes 2000 s. Fast on everything plus accurate on 5% takes $40 + 100 = 140$ s, a 14.3 times speed-up. The accurate fraction dominates: halving it to 2.5% gives $40 + 50 = 90$ s. A tighter fast mode shrinks the ambiguous fraction, so investment in fast-mode accuracy, for example better calibration, pays directly in loop speed. The risk is the reverse: an error bound that is too optimistic lets wrong verdicts through, and the agent closes paths that reopen at signoff. Final signoff always uses the accurate engine on the whole design.

label: Differential parasitic checks for ECOs
lesson:
# Differential parasitic checks for ECOs

When an agent claims that an ECO rerouted three nets, the claim is checkable: re-extract, compare every net's parasitics before and after, and confirm that only the claimed nets and their geometric neighbours moved. This differential parasitic check is the golden test for extraction-level changes. It turns an agent's narrative into a verified diff and catches the side effects that make late ECOs dangerous.

## Which nets moved

Extract the design before and after the ECO with the same extractor version, corner and calibration tables, so that the only difference is the layout change. For each net, compare total capacitance (and, for a thorough check, resistance and each coupling). A net has moved if its change exceeds a tolerance chosen above numerical noise, for example 0.02 fF. With six nets changing $8.1 \to 6$, $2.9 \to 2.9$, $5.8 \to 6.4$, $1.5 \to 0.1$, $1 \to 1$ and $2.1 \to 2.1$ fF, three moved. Determinism matters: if extracting the same layout twice gives different values, the tolerance must absorb that noise and small real effects disappear. That is why extractor seams must be deterministic and seedable.

## Unexpected movers

The ECO's claim defines the expected set: the rerouted nets plus their geometric neighbours, whose coupling legitimately changes when a wire moves beside them. A moved net outside that set is an unexpected mover, evidence that the ECO touched more than it claimed, for example an accidental reroute, a deleted via, or a fill change. Each must be reported with its geometry and change so that an engineer or agent can tell a real side effect from an incomplete expectation, such as a neighbour the claim forgot. The neighbour set itself is computed geometrically by the extractor, from the old and new routes, so that the agent cannot widen it to hide a side effect.

## The pass rule

Two kinds of failure count. Every unexpected mover is one. Every claimed net that did not move is another: if the ECO says it rerouted a net and its parasitics are unchanged, the reroute did not happen or did nothing, and the claim is wrong. With four unexpected movers and one claimed net unchanged, the check reports five failures. The ECO is accepted only at zero. This mirrors the differential timing check for timing engines, and the two compose: the parasitic diff proves the change was confined, and a differential timing report on the new parasitics proves its effect on slack was the intended one. Together they are the evidence an agent hands a human reviewer.

## Going deeper

The golden and differential testing practice described in the agent-first EDA material of this curriculum; McKeeman, "Differential testing for software", Digital Technical Journal (1998).

label: Agentic signoff and ECO loops
lesson:
# Agentic signoff and ECO loops

An agentic signoff loop reads the engines' reports, timing and SI violations, IR and EM hot spots, DRC markers, proposes ECOs, runs them through extraction and analysis, and iterates until the checklist is clean, with a human approving the final change. The engines stay the source of truth; the agent's job is to search and to assemble evidence. Designing that loop safely means deciding what the agent reads, what it may change, how it uses fast and accurate engines, and how it avoids gaming its own metrics.

## Reports in, verified ECOs out

The agent reads typed reports, not raw layout: lists of violating paths with slacks and delta delays, victims with their aggressors and coupling, IR-drop maps, EM violations, DRC markers. It proposes a fix, for example moving a victim to a free track or upsizing a holding driver, and the harness applies it, re-extracts the touched region and re-runs timing, SI, EM/IR and DRC there. Only a change that passes these checks is shown to a human, as a reviewable diff with its evidence. The human approves the final ECO; the agent never writes to the tape-out database directly. Engines exposed as tools with typed inputs and outputs, for example over MCP, make this loop possible without the agent reading engine source.

## Guarding against bad loops

Two failure modes dominate. Oscillation: a setup fix breaks hold, the hold fix breaks setup, and the loop cycles. The loop must detect repeated states and either propose joint fixes, such as delaying the short path while speeding the long one, or escalate. Reward hacking: an agent rewarded for fewer violations may learn to add false-path exceptions or relax margins, which removes violations without fixing anything. Constraints and signoff margins define what correct means, so changes to them must be blocked or require explicit human approval. A differential re-extraction and SI report, showing that only the intended nets and their neighbours changed, is the check that a physical fix did not create new victims elsewhere.

## Fast engines, accurate signoff, and the flywheel

Inside the loop the agent uses fast extraction and timing to rank candidates, and recurses to accurate extraction when a net's slack is within its fast-mode error bound: 2 ps of slack with a 5 ps bound is not a pass. Final signoff always runs the accurate engines on the whole design. The loop runs in a sandbox on the customer's site, with CPU, memory and time limits and no network, because layouts and parasitics must not leave the IP boundary. Batches are kept small enough to verify and roll back. When a fix pattern keeps working across projects, such as spacing-based coupling fixes on clock nets, it is validated with golden and differential tests and promoted into a library skill; the know-how flows back, the customer's design does not.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA domain of this curriculum, on harness loops, change tiers and the skill flywheel; the OpenROAD documentation on its Tcl and Python interfaces, which expose engines as callable tools.
